prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: Operating and Financial Metrics (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Metric" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 407px
  col 2: header "FY 2022" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 61px
  col 3: header "FY 2023" · longest unbreakable word 62px · one-line width 62px
  col 4: header "FY 2024" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 61px
  col 5: header "Q1 2025" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

Row rhythm is even and the eye can run across the numbers; only the last column falls outside the box, which is unavoidable here and handled by scrolling."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Figures all stay intact and headers are on one line, but the Metric column is tighter (~120px) so the long labels stack 4–5 lines, making rows taller and less even than A; the third visible column is clipped mid-header ('FY 20'), which reads as an accident rather than a deliberate scroll point."},"C":{"grade":"poor","why":"Squeezing the Metric column to ~80px forces 5–7 line labels while the year columns (~70px) break number+unit across lines ('$318.4' / 'M'), destroying the integrity of the identifiers; tall ragged rows make cross-row comparison of the figures hard."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"The Metric column is so narrow (~55px) that words split mid-word ('revenu e', 'retenti on', 'month s', 'Custo mer', 'blende d'), and numbers are broken onto two lines everywhere; the table is effectively unreadable and the row unit collapses."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Values remain intact on one line, which saves it, but the Metric column (~95px) wraps into 5–6 lines and the 'FY 2024' header itself breaks across two lines, so the header hierarchy looks unstable and rows become very tall."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Similar to A: generous Metric column gives 3–4 clean line wraps, all figures and units stay together on one line, and headers read straight across.
